As with many AI tools, getting a single recommendation based on a complex set of data made me wonder several things in each case
1) What features is the AI looking at.  If it is giving me a response different from my first response, is that because I am missing something in the case, or because it is not considering the same set of data that I am, or is it because in a large data set it can see correlations between data points that lead to a particular outcome that are statistically apparent but don't align with my physiology based linear thinking? In some cases this was a useful prompt to think about things differently, but when I really disagreed it made me wonder if I am completely misinterpreting the data.
2) When a "best" response is given, it makes me wonder about the incremental benefit of the "best" approach vs others.  That is, is the approach only marginally superior in such a way that even a small change in the data or patient condition would suggest a different approach? 
3) It would be very helpful to have some idea of what factors the AI is weighting in this scenario that lead to this outcome.  There is always measurement uncertainty or the possibility of rapid change in some of the underlying data in the scenario, and I also really have no understanding of whether the AI is looking at trends over time in the assessment.  I was trained to always ask "what if a single piece of data I have is wrong - would it change my plan significantly" to avoid anchoring and premature closure.  I have no understanding if the AI is robust to those types of concerns.
Q18.5: Ideally, AI would not just give me a recommendation, but situate the data extracted from a certain situation within the framework of evidence based or at least guideline based care.  With just a recommendation, I am left doubting my own decision and second guessing myself without a real understanding of where I might differ from the AI decision, which is just frustrating.
